To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

fishing-induced selection for slow somatic growth in European eel is consistent with the hypothesis that fast-growing individuals are less likely to survive until maturity than slow-growing individuals under natural conditions.

fishing mortality can select for slow body growth rates in the European eel (a species with a panmictictic population), and that this may have negative consequences for the species’ reproductive success and population dynamics.

(i) the growth rates of eels are genetically determined; (ii) fast-growing individuals have an advantage over slow-growing individuals under natural conditions (i.e. in the absence of fisheries); (iii) fishing mortality can select for slower growth rates by removing faster growing individuals from the population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (i) Does fishing mortality induce adaptive responses in growth rates of fishes?
the effects of fisheries on the evolution of growth in fishes.
the effects of fishing on the evolution of life-history traits of fishes, with a particular emphasis on body growth rate and its consequences for population dynamics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
fishing-induced selection for slow somatic growth in European eel is a reality.
fishery-induced selection for slow growth in European eel is not a remote possibility but a likely outcome of the intensive exploitation of this species.
the European eel is not a single species, but a group of several species, and that each of these species is in danger of extinction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the European eel is a species that has been exploited for centuries, and the exploitation has led to a dramatic decline.

fishing can induce adaptive responses on body growth in fishes, but this is not a common phenomenon and the magnitude of the effect depends on the life history of the species, fishing intensity, and other environmental factors.
the intensive exploitation of European eel has led to a decrease in the growth rate of eel populations, which is a consequence of human-induced evolution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of fishing on the evolution of growth rates should be carefully considered when designing conservation strategies for exploited species.
fishing-induced evolution should be taken into account in the management of exploited populations.
fisheries management can affect evolutionary trajectories of exploited populations.
